analysis.title: November update - CIO View: Commodities
key_insights: UBS CIO says the CMCI Commodity Total Return Index is up more than 30% since the start of the year. It sees commodities as a structural source of returns and as portfolio protection when rising inflation expectations pressure equities and bonds.

UBS recommends diversified commodity exposure across precious metals, energy, industrial metals and agriculture. It favors an actively managed approach because leadership within commodities is shifting quickly.
The longer-term backdrop is supported by electrification, rising power demand, AI infrastructure investment and supply constraints in several markets.
Middle Eastern oil exports have recovered but remain below pre-conflict levels, leaving the oil market undersupplied and vulnerable to renewed regional tensions.

Further strategic oil reserve releases by OECD states should help contain near-term price spikes by offsetting commercial inventory declines. The relief is temporary and does not remove the underlying tightness. Drawing down emergency stocks could also mean larger price swings after future supply disruptions.

Gold has fallen as higher US real yields and a stronger US dollar raise the opportunity cost of holding it. UBS says gold has held up well against the rise in yields, and its sensitivity to real rates has weakened because structural demand offsets more than in past cycles.

UBS expects annual central bank gold purchases of 750-1,000 metric tons. September purchases kept a solid pace on preliminary data. Other supports are concern about public debt and debt-servicing costs, an expected weaker US dollar over time, and robust Chinese buying.

Near term, gold may retest support around USD 4,000/oz, where UBS expects structural dip buyers to set a floor. It expects gold to stabilize and resume its uptrend toward year-end and into 2027 as the market reassesses further Fed tightening and real yields fall.
UBS says pullbacks toward USD 4,000/oz offer opportunities to add gold exposure. It keeps a mid-single-digit gold allocation as appropriate for investors who like real assets.

Base metals are well supported despite a weak macro backdrop, but UBS expects performance to diverge across the complex. It is constructive on copper and aluminum and cautious on nickel, lead and zinc, which have less favorable balances.
Copper is UBS's preferred metal. Mine-supply growth keeps disappointing, concentrate availability is exceptionally tight, and LME and SHFE inventories are declining.
Headlines about a possible Cobre Panama restart have weighed on copper sentiment, but there is no clarity on timing, scale or legal pathway, so little near-term relief for the physical market.
US tariff uncertainty distorts regional copper flows. Inventories are concentrated in the US while availability outside the US stays tight.

Chinese refined copper demand stays resilient despite high prices and a weak property sector, supported by power grid, renewables, EV and industrial investment. Elevated Yangshan premiums and SHFE inventory drawdowns point to the same.

sector_views.rationale: Structural demand from central banks, China and debt concerns supports gold. UBS expects a floor near USD 4,000/oz and a resumed uptrend toward year-end and 2027.
Oil exports from the Middle East remain below pre-conflict levels, so the market is undersupplied. Strategic reserve releases give only temporary relief.
Constrained supply, lean inventories and electrification and infrastructure demand support both. Copper is the preferred metal.
UBS describes the supply-demand balances for these metals as less favorable and takes a more cautious stance.
